title: “GIVE AND GOD WILL MAKE YOU RICH” — IS THAT REALLY THE GOSPEL?
paragraphs: “GIVE AND GOD WILL MAKE YOU RICH” — IS THAT REALLY THE GOSPEL?
What if the most dangerous lie about giving is not that God wants your money… but that He owes you more money when you give it?
There is a version of Christianity that sounds almost irresistible.
Give, and your bank account will grow.
Sow a seed, and your financial breakthrough will come.
Send the offering, and God will multiply it back.
Give enough, believe hard enough, speak positively enough—and eventually heaven will have no choice but to make you wealthy.
It sounds spiritual.
It uses Bible verses.
It mentions faith.
It talks about blessing.
Sometimes it even uses the name of Jesus.
And that is exactly why the question matters.
Because not everything that says “Jesus” is the Gospel Jesus preached.
Imagine a woman sitting alone at her kitchen table late at night.
The house is quiet, but her mind is not.
There are bills beside her.
A nearly empty bank account on her phone.
A child asleep in the next room.
A prayer she has prayed so many times that she no longer knows whether she is praying or simply crying.
Then she hears a preacher say:
“Give tonight. Sow into this ministry. God is about to return it to you multiplied.”
She looks at what little she has.
And something happens inside her.
Hope.
Fear.
Desperation.
Maybe this is the answer.
Maybe this is the miracle.
Maybe if she gives God what she cannot afford to lose, God will finally give her what she desperately needs.
So she gives.
Not because she has suddenly become overwhelmed by love for Christ.
Not because she freely wants to help the poor.
Not because the Gospel has made her generous.
She gives because she has quietly been taught to treat the offering plate like an investment account.
And God like the guarantor.
That is where something beautiful can become terribly distorted.
Biblical generosity is beautiful.
Sacrificial giving is biblical.
Supporting Gospel ministry is biblical.
Caring for pastors and teachers is biblical.
Feeding the hungry, helping struggling believers, caring for widows, supporting missionaries, serving the poor, and using our possessions for the kingdom of God are profoundly biblical.
But “give money to God and He is obligated to make you financially rich” is not the Gospel.
In fact, Scripture gives us a chilling warning about turning Christianity into a method of financial gain.
Paul speaks about people who imagine:
“πορισμὸν εἶναι τὴν εὐσέβειαν”
porismon einai tēn eusebeian—
that godliness is a means of gain.
Then comes the stunning correction:
“ἔστιν δὲ πορισμὸς μέγας ἡ εὐσέβεια μετὰ αὐταρκείας.”
“But godliness with contentment is great gain.”
That is 1 Timothy 6:5–6.
Notice what Paul does.
He does not say Christianity is the secret to getting more.
He confronts the idea that godliness should be treated as a mechanism for material profit, and then redefines “gain” around godliness joined with contentment.
And a few verses later he writes:
Then:
“If we have food and clothing, with these we will be content.”
That does not sound like a divine get-rich formula.
It sounds like freedom.
Because Jesus did not die to turn your greed religious.
He died to set you free from being owned by it.
That distinction cuts deeply because prosperity teaching can take a genuine biblical truth—God is generous—and quietly turn it into something Scripture never promised.
Yes, God provides.
Yes, God blesses.
Yes, God answers prayer.
Yes, every good gift ultimately comes from Him.
Yes, Scripture contains examples of people whom God entrusted with substantial wealth.
Abraham had wealth.
Job had wealth.
David had wealth.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wealth.
There is nothing inherently sinful about possessing money.
But there is an enormous difference between saying, “God may entrust wealth to someone,” and saying, “God promises financial wealth to everyone who gives money in faith.”
The first can be demonstrated from Scripture.
The second cannot.
Jesus Himself said:
“Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions.”
Luke 12:15.
Read that slowly.
Your life does not consist in the abundance of what you possess.
The culture says, “More.”
Greed says, “More.”
Consumerism says, “More.”
The distorted prosperity message can baptize the same hunger and say:
“More—but now call it blessing.”
Jesus says your life is not there.
And then there is the rich young ruler.
If the Gospel were fundamentally a pathway toward material accumulation, Jesus had a strange way of recruiting wealthy followers.
He told the man to relinquish what had captured his heart.
The tragedy was not merely that the man possessed wealth.
The tragedy was that wealth possessed him.
He walked away sorrowful.
Why?
Because Jesus touched the throne.
That is what the real Gospel does.
It does not merely ask what is in your wallet.
It exposes what is on your throne.
And sometimes the most revealing question is not, “How much money do I have?”
It is:
“What would happen to my faith if God never made me rich?”
Would Jesus still be enough?
If your income did not double…
if the promotion never arrived…
if the business struggled…
if the miracle took longer than expected…
if obedience cost you instead of enriching you…
would Christ still be worthy?
That question separates worship from transaction.
Some people do not really want God.
They want what they believe God can give them.
And if we are not careful, Christian language can hide that reality even from ourselves.
“Bless me.”
“Expand me.”
“Prosper me.”
“Increase me.”
None of those desires are automatically sinful.
But underneath them there can be another prayer we are afraid to say aloud:
“Jesus, I want You because I think You can get me the life I really want.”
Then Jesus comes near and asks:
“What if I am the treasure?”
That is Christianity.
Not Jesus as the key to your treasure.
Jesus as the Treasure.
This is why one of the most frequently quoted giving passages deserves to be heard in its actual context.
Second Corinthians 9 says:
“Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.”
True.
Absolutely true.
But keep reading.
Paul says each person should give as he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not under compulsion.
That matters.
Christian giving is not supposed to be extracted through spiritual intimidation.
It is not supposed to be driven by someone making frightened people believe that refusing to send money will cause God to withhold their miracle.
Paul continues by speaking of God providing sufficiency so believers may abound in every good work, and of being enriched so they may be generous.
Do you see the direction?
God's provision does not terminate on the giver.
It creates generosity.
The biblical picture is not:
“I give so I can accumulate.”
It is:
“God provides so I can keep becoming generous.”
The blessing becomes a river instead of a reservoir.
And yes, God can provide materially.
He can open doors no human being could open.
He can give employment.
He can rescue a business.
He can provide through another believer.
He can give extraordinary opportunities.
He can entrust significant resources to someone whose hands remain open.
We should never reduce God's ability to provide.
But neither should we turn His sovereignty into a vending machine.
Put money in.
Select blessing.
Press faith.
Wait for prosperity.
God is not manipulated by formulas.
Grace cannot be purchased.
And faith is not a currency with which we force heaven into debt.
Perhaps someone is thinking about Malachi:
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse…”
Then God speaks of opening “the windows of heaven.”
That text is real.
The promise is real.
But so is its covenantal and historical context.

Malachi is addressing covenant unfaithfulness among Israel, including matters surrounding tithes and the storehouse. We should learn from the passage about God's faithfulness, obedience, worship, and generosity, but we should not carelessly convert it into a universal New Covenant promise that every Christian who transfers money to a ministry will receive a predetermined financial return.
The New Testament does not teach believers to give ten dollars so God owes them one hundred.
It teaches something far more radical.
Give because Christ gave Himself.
Give freely.
Give cheerfully.
Give sacrificially.
Give wisely.
Give to meet genuine needs.
Give to advance faithful Gospel ministry.
Give without making God your debtor.
And give because money is a terrible savior.
Jesus said:
“You cannot serve God and money.”
Not because money is inherently evil.
Money can feed someone.
Money can put Scripture into someone's hands.
Money can support a missionary.
Money can pay a struggling family's electricity bill.
Money can fund Gospel work.
Money can build hospitals, shelters, churches, schools, and ministries.
Money is a tool.
But it makes a merciless master.
Paul did not say money itself was the root of all evil. First Timothy 6:10 speaks of φιλαργυρία — philargyria, the love of money.
That distinction matters.
You can have money without worshiping it.
And you can have very little money while desperately worshiping the idea of having more.
The Gospel confronts both hearts.
Then someone quotes 2 Corinthians 8:9:
“Though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich.”
There it is, they say.
Jesus became poor so Christians could become rich.
But what kind of riches is Paul unfolding?
Read the surrounding chapters.
Paul is calling believers into grace-filled generosity. Christ's self-giving becomes the supreme pattern. The One who possessed heavenly glory humbled Himself for us.
To turn that breathtaking revelation of Christ's grace into “Jesus became poor so I can get a luxury lifestyle” shrinks something glorious into something painfully small.
Christ became poor for us so impoverished sinners could receive the riches of His grace.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
Adoption.
Righteousness in Christ.
Eternal life.
The Holy Spirit.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.
God Himself.
And this is where the prosperity message becomes especially heartbreaking.
Because Christianity already promises riches beyond imagination.
We simply became so fascinated with temporary riches that eternal riches began to look ordinary.
Imagine standing before Christ with every earthly thing you ever begged for.
The house.
The car.
The clothes.
The investments.
The recognition.
The business.
The vacations.
The status.
Then imagine having all of it…
and not having Him.
Would you call yourself rich?
Jesus asked:
“What does it profit a man to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?”
The whole world.
Not merely a million dollars.
The world.
And Jesus says you could gain it and still lose.
There are people with almost nothing who possess treasure that death cannot touch.
And there are people surrounded by luxury who are spiritually bankrupt.
This does not mean poverty is automatically holy.
Poverty can involve terrible suffering, injustice, hunger, exploitation, and pain. Christians should care deeply about relieving it.
Nor does wealth automatically make someone wicked.

Scripture instructs wealthy believers not necessarily to become destitute, but not to become arrogant or place their hope in uncertain riches. They are to be rich in good works, generous, and ready to share.
The issue is lordship.
Who owns whom?
That question eventually reaches all of us.
Because prosperity theology is easy to criticize when a television preacher is asking for money.
It becomes harder when we discover a tiny prosperity preacher living inside our own hearts.
“I obeyed You, God. Why did this happen?”
“I gave. Why am I still struggling?”
“I served You. Why did someone else get promoted?”
“I prayed. Why didn't You fix it?”
“I stayed faithful. Why did You allow me to lose this?”
Behind those questions there can be real pain.
God is not offended by honest lament. Scripture is filled with it.
But sometimes underneath our disappointment lies an agreement we thought God signed:
“I will follow You if You make my life work.”
Then suffering arrives.
And suddenly we discover what kind of gospel we believed.
The apostles followed Jesus.
They were not promised comfortable lives.
Paul knew hunger.
Thirst.
Beatings.
Imprisonment.
Shipwreck.
Danger.
Sleepless nights.
Cold.
Exposure.

Jesus Himself said that those who follow Him receive a new kingdom family and God's provision, yet Mark 10:30 includes two words that prosperity slogans have difficulty putting on fundraising banners:
μετὰ διωγμῶν — meta diōgmōn.
“With persecutions.”
Jesus did not hide the cost.
He did not need manipulation to make disciples.
He told people to count it.
Take up your cross.
Follow Me.
Lose your life and find it.
The symbol at the center of Christianity is not a money bag.
It is a cross.
And at that cross, the greatest transaction in history took place—but you did not finance it.
You could not.
I could not.
We were the bankrupt ones.
Spiritually unable to purchase our redemption.
Then Christ paid what we could never pay.
Not with silver.
Not with gold.
With Himself.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
We sinned.
He was righteous.
We wandered.
He came looking.
We accumulated guilt.
He carried it.
We deserved judgment.
He offered mercy.
We could not purchase forgiveness.
So Jesus purchased us.
The Gospel is not that you give something to God so God becomes obligated to enrich you.
The Gospel is that God gave His Son for sinners who could never repay Him.
That changes giving completely.
Now I do not give to manipulate God.
I give because God has already been unimaginably generous toward me.
I do not give to purchase His love.
I give because in Christ I have received love I could never purchase.
I do not give because someone frightened me into believing my miracle depends on my payment.
I give because grace has loosened my grip.
I do not ask, “How little can I give and still receive a blessing?”
Grace teaches me to ask:
“Jesus, everything I have belongs to You. How can I use it faithfully?”
That may mean supporting a church faithfully preaching Christ.
Helping a missionary.
Buying groceries for a struggling family.
Supporting a trustworthy Christian ministry.
Helping someone without announcing it.
Opening your home.
Feeding someone hungry.
Giving your time.
Giving your skills.
Giving financially.
Giving secretly.
Giving sacrificially.
Sometimes giving until you actually feel the sacrifice.
But never because God can be bribed.
Never because salvation is for sale.
Never because a ministry has convinced you that supporting it is a condition of God's favor.
Even Gospel Warrior must never become your mediator.
Jesus is.
Buying a Christian book cannot make God love you.
Sharing this article cannot purchase a blessing.
Supporting this ministry cannot earn forgiveness.
Christ alone saves.
Grace alone is the reason a sinner can come home.

And precisely because that is true, believers can freely choose to support ministries that genuinely help them grow and spread biblical truth—not as payment to God, but as participation in Gospel work.
Not because God will love you more if you do.
Not because heaven owes you money afterward.
But because when something faithfully points people toward Christ, helping it reach another person can itself become an act of generosity.
Not as a spiritual transaction.
As a mission.
Someone scrolling tonight may have spent years believing God abandoned them because they gave and never became wealthy.
Someone may secretly think their financial struggle proves their faith is defective.
Someone may have walked away from Christianity because a distorted message promised them prosperity and left them disappointed with God.
Send this to that person.
And if this exposed something in your own heart, do not hide behind religious language.
“Jesus, be my treasure.”
Maybe your confession is simpler.
“No more transactions. I want Christ.”
Your honesty may become permission for someone else to stop pretending.
Because there will probably come a day when disappointment whispers:
“If God really loved you, wouldn't He have given you more?”
Come back and remember:
Calvary already answered whether God loves you.
The cross was never God's promise that Christians would become financially wealthy.
It was something infinitely greater.
God giving Himself to rescue sinners.
It is not purchasing spiritual status.

It is simply one practical way, for those who are able and willing, to support the continued creation and sharing of Christ-centered resources while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, discipleship, encouragement, accountability, and spiritual sharpening.
Open your Bible.
Test what you hear.
Know Christ.
Repent when He exposes sin.
Receive His grace.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Give because you have received.
Serve because Christ served you.
Love because He first loved you.
And when God gives you much, hold it with open hands.
When He gives you little, do not assume you have been abandoned.
When He provides unexpectedly, thank Him.
When He allows a season of scarcity, cling to Him.
When your prayers are answered differently from what you imagined, do not confuse disappointment with divine absence.
Your greatest evidence of God's generosity is not parked in your driveway.
It happened on a hill outside Jerusalem.
A bloodied Savior.
A wooden cross.
A borrowed tomb.
And then—
an empty grave.
That is our wealth.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ returning.
The Gospel does not promise that everyone who follows Jesus will become financially rich.
It promises something money could never buy:
the guilty can be forgiven.
The lost can be found.
The ashamed can be covered.
The rebellious can be reconciled.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The sinner can become a child of God.
And the person whose entire story looks ruined can discover that Jesus has not reached the final sentence yet.
So give.
Give generously.
Give joyfully.
Give wisely.
Give sacrificially when Christ leads you to sacrifice.
Support faithful Gospel work.
Share truth.
Help people.
Feed people.
Strengthen believers.
Reach unbelievers.
Use your resources for things eternity will remember.
But never reduce the King of heaven to an investment strategy.
God does not owe you riches because you gave Him money.
In Christ, He has already offered you a treasure greater than the world could ever deposit into your hands.
And perhaps that is the sentence we need to carry with us long after this page closes:
If Jesus Himself is not enough for us, no amount of blessing will ever make us rich.
